extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, historians of mathematics, and mathematicians interested in the methodology and epistemology of proof and conjecture
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and evaluation of how mathematical conjectures are produced, proved, criticised, and how definitions and concepts change in response to counterexamples; emphasizes the dialectic of proofs and refutations. Targeted at methodological reflection rather than providing formal proof techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof as thought-experiment / quasi-experiment
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'proof' may be a thought-experiment or 'quasi-experiment' which suggests a decomposition of the original conjecture into subconjectures or lemmas, thus embedding it in a possibly quite distant body of knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat proofs not only as final, infallible demonstrations but also as heuristic constructions that expose hidden lemmas and connect conjectures to broader theories. Example: the teacher's rubber-sheet thought-experiment that reduces a polyhedron to a planar triangulated network; it 'proved' the conjecture only by decomposing it into further lemmas (some of which may be false). Scoring note: distinguish the heuristic value of such a proof from its establishing absolute truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local vs global counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between 'local counterexamples' (which refute a lemma/subconjecture used in a proof but not necessarily the main conjecture) and 'global counterexamples' (which refute the main conjecture itself).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a proof or conjecture, identify whether an objection targets an embedded lemma (local) or the conjecture as a whole (global). Local counterexamples indicate faults in the proof-analysis and suggest lemma-revision; global ones force reconsideration of the conjecture. Example: removing an interior triangle from a triangulated net is a local counterexample to a triangle-removal lemma but not to Euler's formula itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of surrender (rejection of the conjecture)
rubrics_metrics.description: One possible response to a global counterexample is surrender: abandon or reject the conjecture when a genuine global refutation is found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat surrender as a legitimate methodological move when counterexamples demonstrate the conjecture false across its intended domain. It is the straightforward rational response to unrefutable global counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of monster-barring (rejecting the counterexample)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject the counterexample by labeling it a 'monster' (i.e. outside the intended concept) and exclude it via ad hoc redefinition or restrictive stipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monster-barring is an ad hoc stratagem that exorcises counterexamples by contracting the concept (e.g. redefining 'polyhedron' so that the picture-frame is no longer a polyhedron). Critique: this can be dogmatic and stifle genuine conceptual growth; use with caution. Example: Delta's redefinition to exclude tunnel-like 'picture-frame' solids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improving conjecture by exception-barring (piecemal exclusions / strategic withdrawal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Modify the conjecture to exclude the troublesome cases (add exceptions) — a controlled form of narrowing the conjecture's scope to avoid counterexamples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception-barring can salvage useful generalizations by explicitly restricting domains; but it risks becoming a long list of ad hoc exclusions. Prefer principled restrictions when possible. Terms used in the paper: 'piecemeal exclusions' and 'strategic withdrawal.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of monster-adjustment
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjust the description or interpretation of the counterexample so that it no longer refutes the conjecture without simply excluding it; i.e. transform the monster so it fits the theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monster-adjustment differs from monster-barring by altering the monster's status or properties rather than contracting the concept. Use when there is a plausible, non-ad hoc reinterpretation that preserves explanatory power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improving conjecture by lemma-incorporation (proof-generated theorem versus naive conjecture)
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate lemmas discovered during proof-analysis into an improved formulation of the theorem; accept that the theorem one 'proves' may be a different (often stronger or more complex) statement than the naive conjecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that proofs can generate new, more precise theorems; good methodology accepts proof-generated reformulations as legitimate outcomes. Example: transforming the original Euler conjecture by adding conditions discovered during attempted proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof must make its hidden conditions explicit (avoid unstated restrictions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A valid proof must not rely on unstated assumptions or hidden restrictions; any conditions used (e.g., 'boundary triangle' or 'removal order that preserves V-E+F') must be explicitly stated and justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a proof, identify all tacit lemmas and check whether they hold for the whole intended class; if a counterexample exploits an unstated restriction, the proof-analysis must be corrected or the conjecture reformulated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic precedence: conjecture (guess) precedes proof
rubrics_metrics.description: In mathematical discovery the conjecture (the guess) comes before the proof; proofs often follow from creative guesses, not the other way around.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological frameworks should support and study the heuristic processes that generate conjectures. Acceptance of a theorem is a process: first conjecture, then testing, then attempted proof, then criticism and refinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refutations fuel proof-elaboration and theorem-formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Refutations and counterexamples play a constructive role: they reveal weaknesses, force re-analysis of proofs, inspire lemma generation, and contribute to concept and theorem evolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the quality of mathematical practice by how it uses refutations productively: not by exorcising them, but by revising proofs, definitions, and conjectures. Example: local counterexamples led to modified lemma statements and improved proof strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallibilism: mathematics is corrigible and revisable
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical knowledge, especially informal mathematics, is fallible; proofs and conjectures are subject to revision in the light of criticism and new counterexamples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a fallibilist stance in methodological evaluation: avoid treating 'proof' as absolute finality; instead view it as part of an ongoing critical methodology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concept-formation should be responsive but principled
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions and concepts (e.g. 'polyhedron', 'polygon') evolve in response to counterexamples, but redefinitions must be principled rather than merely ad hoc devices to rescue cherished theorems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing conceptual changes, check whether the new definition captures the intended phenomena and offers explanatory or classificatory virtues, rather than just excluding dissenting examples. Example: debate over various definitions (Defs. 1–6) of 'polyhedron' and the merits of each.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat monsters with respect — they can be 'hopeful monsters'
rubrics_metrics.description: Pathological or 'monster' counterexamples, though initially dismissed, can catalyse conceptual innovation and open fruitful new lines of inquiry ('hopeful monsters').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't reflexively dismiss anomalies; evaluate whether a monster suggests a valuable generalization or a need for deeper theory. Historical note: monsters spurred developments in function theory and topology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer non-arbitrary over arbitrary fixes (avoid surreptitious shifts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodological improvements should avoid surreptitious or ad hoc shifts of position (e.g., saying 'I meant...' to retroactively salvage a proof); instead, make transparent, justified revisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a proof or lemma is refuted, explicitly state the replacement claim and rationale. Intellectual honesty requires overt reformulation rather than covert reinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions can be explicit or implicit and need empirical/structural tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions may be stated explicitly (syntactic clauses) or implicitly (characterizing structural/behavioural properties, e.g. the cross-section criterion for polyhedra). Each form should be tested against canonical and boundary cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a proposed definition, test it with constructed examples (cubes, hollow cubes, picture-frames, cylinders, star-polygons) to see whether it captures intended cases and excludes pathological ones for principled reasons. Example: Def. 5 (implicit cross-section criterion) was proposed to exclude picture-frame monsters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reductive structures (using reductions in theorem analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek reductive analyses that break complex conjectures into simpler components or reduce them to previously understood results; use such structures in proof-elaboration and in explaining how refutations affect the theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether a proposed reduction genuinely preserves the problem's essential structure and whether counterexamples reveal faults in the reductive step. Reductive proofs must be scrutinized for hidden assumptions that local counterexamples may expose.
